title: Oil slicks in the Strait of Hormuz are harming the environment
summary: More than 600 oil slicks threaten marine life in the Strait of Hormuz as war and tanker attacks turn vital waters into an environmental disaster.

Sponsor Message Transcript JUANA SUMMERS, HOST: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps has been attacking oil tankers at a record pace. The IRGC says it's hitting several tankers a day. That's despite U.S. military efforts to guide ships through the Strait of Hormuz. NPR's Aya Batrawy saw oil washing ashore in the nearby United Arab Emirates. (SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING) AYA BATRAWY, BYLINE: It's a bright and sunny day here in Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates. And this beach is open, there's families here, the water is clear. But there are several stretches of the beach in the United Arab Emirates that are now closed because of oil spills because Iran continues to attack oil tankers trying to go in or out of the Strait of Hormuz. (SOUNDBITE OF CHILDREN PLAYING) BATRAWY: The U.N. has tracked around 150 attacks on ships since the start of the war. Greenpeace says its satellite monitoring has identified more than 600 possible oil slicks across Gulf waters from these attacks and the war, stretching some 8,000 square miles. Inesaf Benzaki is a campaigner with Greenpeace Middle East and North Africa. INESAF BENZAKI: It is really the repeated aspect of it in such a small area that compounds the scale of the damage. And yes, of course long-term monitoring, environmental monitoring is essential. But we can gauge that recovery will need a lot of time. BATRAWY: She says the damage from these repeated oil spills is not only harming marine life and sensitive ecosystems like mangroves, but also the food chain and drinking water supplies the Gulf relies on. One of Iran's attacks on October 2 struck a ship carrying 2 million barrels of crude. That oil washed up on the UAE's shores a couple weeks later. The entire coast of the emirate of Umm Al Quwain has been closed to the public ever since. The sand has dark brown hues, and the smell of oil permeates the air. I can see a clean-up crew. I can see men in, you know, these hazard outfits cleaning up the coast. There's some kind of generator running and a hose to sort of suck, I guess, the oil, the petrol out of the water. To draw attention to the environmental costs of the war, British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh swam in the Strait of Hormuz this month. Pugh describes the experience for The Associated Press. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) LEWIS PUGH: I heard two very loud explosions. They literally rocked the sea. And I looked up, and I could see that an oil tanker about 4 kilometers away had been hit. BATRAWY: But that's not all he saw. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) PUGH: As we sailed in there, we're seeing so many dolphins following our boats. We see turtles and then big ospreys. It's literally one of the treasure troves of the natural world. BATRAWY: A treasure trove that is also a lifeline for the Gulf and that is being harmed every day that the war goes on. Aya Batrawy, NPR News, the UAE. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information.
